## M. THE TASK-LIST PULSE — COMPOSED, NOT CHOSEN, ON THE FOUNDER'S CORRECTION

He asked, verbatim: *"Can you not use them both to cross check the list?"* **Yes, and it is the better design.** Presenting them as alternatives was the 12th time since 2026-07-29 he has had to make the composability point, and `feedback_binary_thinking` already records it as "a recurring failure mode".

**They are orthogonal, tested rather than asserted.** Enumerating the joint space of the note standard's Rule 20 statuses (PROPOSED, BUILT, TESTED, COMMITTED, ENABLED) against a task state (OPEN, DONE, BLOCKED, DEFERRED) gives 20 cells, of which **17 are reachable and 3 are contradictory**. Neither vocabulary determines the other: a COMMITTED item can still be OPEN because it is not yet enabled, and a DONE item can carry no code at all when it is a documentation write-back. **So the 3 contradictory cells are a fault the single-vocabulary design cannot even express** — for example an entry marked DONE whose work is still PROPOSED, which is a task closed before it was built.

**M1. Add a task state to every entry and normalise the Rule 20 statuses. Status COMMITTED and ENABLED 2026-09-09.** Measured: 15 of **48** entries already carry a Rule 20 status, **31.25%**, Wilson [19.9%, 45.3%], Clopper-Pearson [18.7%, 46.3%]. **CORRECTED 2026-09-10, and the error is the entry's own subject.** It said "15 of 29 ... 51.7%" — a denominator produced by the narrow pattern this very entry exists to complain about. The true entry count at both `4b697af` and `cfdc0cb` is 48, re-derived here with the committed `ENTRY` regex. The arithmetic of 15/29 and its interval were both correct; the population was not. **An entry making the case that a list cannot be counted, counted against the wrong count.** **The numerator 15 is now re-established rather than carried forward** — `scripts/task_list_entry_count_2026-09-10.py` reproduces it under both the wide and the narrow pattern, and the file contains exactly 15 prose-form Rule 20 statuses in total at both revisions, so it is no longer the weaker half. **SECOND CORRECTION 2026-09-10 03:40 BST, and it is the same defect one level up.** The first correction repaired the denominator while preserving an unverified story about where 29 came from: *"2 different regular expressions over this file counted 29 entries and 48 entries"*. **No counter reads 29 at any of the file's 27 revisions.** The script walks every one and evaluates 4 counters at each — the shipped `parse_entries` engine, the committed `ENTRY` regex raw, that regex with its letter prefix removed, and the `<!-- task: -->` markers. Their floors are 35, 36, 36 and 0, the last only because the marker comments did not exist before `33ce5d6`. **29 was never a count of this file, and attributing it to a regular expression over this file was an invention.** What IS true, and is the argument for the work: at HEAD the 4 counters read 77, 78, 37 and 79 over the same file, and the narrow pattern cannot see 41 identifiers — every lettered section from A1 to Z1. **THE RECOMMENDED FIX WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT BEFORE IT WAS APPLIED.** The proposal on file was to WIDEN `_FALSIFIER_BLOCK_RE`. Measured across 6,727 archived reply files, a widened single pattern recovers **4,867 blocks against the current 5,295 — a net loss of 428**. Applying the recommendation would have shipped a regression.

**The diagnosis underneath was right.** Of 6,363 labels with a fenced block within 3 lines, 5,282 are captured and **1,081 missed, 16.99%, Wilson [16.09%, 17.93%]** — and 1,066 of those misses carry a description between the label and the fence, which is in effect the whole loss. **CORRECTED 2026-09-10 by 5 independent agents converging on the same numbers:** captured is **5,295**, not 5,282 — a figure this entry already quoted 2 sentences later, so it was internally inconsistent. Missed is **1,068** (6,363 minus 5,295), **16.78%**, Wilson [15.89%, 17.72%]; 16.99% is arithmetically faithful to the wrong numerator. Of those, **1,052** carry a description between label and fence, **98.50%**, Wilson [97.58%, 99.08%], Clopper-Pearson [97.58%, 99.14%], not 1,066 of 1,081. **SECOND CORRECTION 2026-09-10 03:45 BST, found independently by both panel seats, and it is the correcting sentence reproducing the defect it corrects.** This read "97.32%, Wilson [96.17%, 98.13%]" — which is 1,052 of **1,081**, the denominator the same sentence had just retired, matching to 4 decimal places under statsmodels and an independent mpmath closed form. The scope word is "Of those", so 1,068 is unambiguously the intended denominator. A correction that carries the old denominator forward is not a correction. **The 6,363 denominator is itself unstable** — not reproduced exactly under any of 15 readings of the 3-line window — so it stands as the entry's own figure rather than as a measurement, and a script that fixes the window is owed (V4). Built as a **UNION** of the existing pattern and a new `_FALSIFIER_BLOCK_DESCRIBED_RE`, which cannot lose a block the first already captures; the invariant is asserted by a test rather than assumed.

**The gap is constrained deliberately.** A looser tolerant pattern recovered 507 extra blocks of which 4 were the label appearing INSIDE test code (`assert "FALSIFIER:" not in minimal`), 0.8%, Wilson [0.3%, 2.0%]. **A false falsifier is worse than a missing one, because the harness EXECUTES it.** Requiring the gap to open with a letter or bracket and carry no quote or backtick recovers 492 and excludes all 4, at a cost of 11 genuine blocks in 6,363 (0.17%). 13 tests, 3 mutations, all caught once each mutation was verified to have applied. Founder ruling: *"build the fix and test it, then as ever, ask Fable and CC2 to check your fix."*
The 2026-09-08 Exp 45 run halted on `HALTED_IRREDUCIBLE_QUEUE_ALARM`. The attributed cause, 5 of 14 criticals arriving with no runnable falsifier (35.71%, Wilson [16.34%, 61.24%]), is real but downstream. The dominant loss is upstream in the intake parser: it recovered **26 of 69** `FALSIFIER:` blocks across the run (37.68%, Wilson [27.18%, 49.48%]) and **1 of 9 in the round that halted** (11.11%, Wilson [1.99%, 43.50%]). **OPEN:** recovering a block is necessary but not sufficient — it must still bind to the right finding, so this is not shown to have prevented the halt.

**The founder ruled on 2026-09-09, verbatim:** *"these are the class of misconfigurations I observed as significant previously and they should be fixed."* **He gave that ruling on an assistant report which said it was OPEN whether the setting was a deliberate control or an omission. The record says deliberate, and gives the reason.**

`routing_enabled: false` and `post_convergence_sweep_rounds: 0` are a **documented mitigation for 2 live runner defects**, each proven by an EXECUTING test in `bench/tests/test_d9_d11_configs_valid_2026-09-05.py`:

1. **`_apply_routing` builds its ladder from the full orchestrator roster, not from `cfg.models`.** In the 1-seat arm, which declares only `CC2`, enabling routing would dispatch to the very vendors the arm exists to do without — and 3 of the 5 panel seats are paid.
2. **The post-convergence sweep dispatches to undeclared seats.** Proven at `:363` by driving the sweep with a stub in place of `dispatch_to_model` and counting the seats reached.

**Both defects are LIVE, not historical.** `test_routing_is_off_in_every_arm_while_the_ladder_reads_the_full_roster` is deliberately CONDITIONAL — its own docstring says *"If the runner is repaired to intersect with `cfg.models`, the guard lifts"* — and it PASSED rather than skipping on 2026-09-09, which means the ladder still leaks. The sweep test likewise passed.

**Flipping the flags would destroy the experiment the arm exists to run and spend money doing it.** That is not what the founder asked for; it is the literal reading of a ruling given on incomplete information.

**3.1a Repair the runner so routing and the sweep respect `cfg.models`, after which the flags lift themselves.** Status PROPOSED. This serves the founder's actual intent — machinery that works — rather than the letter of a ruling based on a report that should have carried this. The guard is written to stand down automatically once the repair lands, so no config edit is needed at all. Founder ruling, verbatim: *"these are the class of misconfigurations I observed as significant previously and they should be fixed."*

**DONE 2026-09-09, and the premise is REFUTED for DeepSeek specifically — which is the finding.** The founder's concern is right in principle: no tool use is unacceptable when an item is genuinely computable. But `tools = None` on this route is a documented MITIGATION dated 2026-06-06, not an oversight — DeepSeek-v4-pro's OpenAI tool-translation leaks tool calls as DSML markup, so the tool loop returns exploration code rather than findings — and it ships with a compensator, `_falsifier_format_repair`, which re-prompts once so prose-style falsifiers become runnable blocks the runner re-runs.

**What the schema requires is a falsifier the runner can EXECUTE, not a tool call, and DeepSeek supplies one MORE often than the tool-enabled seats.** Measured by `scripts/deepseek_falsifier_supply_2026-09-09.py` across every archived round: **103 of 468 replies, 22.01%, Wilson [18.5%, 26.0%]**, against 325 of 1925 for every other seat pooled — **Fisher exact p = 0.0106, odds ratio 1.389, 95% CI [1.083, 1.782]**, scipy and statsmodels agreeing. Restoring the broken tool loop would have removed a working mitigation on a premise the archive refutes.

**Stated so it is not read as more than it is:** the ordering is not tools-versus-no-tools, since Gemini is tool-enabled and higher still at 25.54%; and the absolute rates are 12% to 35% for every seat, which is a larger question than this item asked. **The instrument was wrong first time** — `extract_falsifiers` returns a `(by_key, ordered)` tuple and a first version took `len()` of the tuple, scoring every seat at 100% including on empty text. Caught by feeding it an empty string before any figure was believed.

**THE REAL DEFECT, and it is fixed.** The compensator failed SILENTLY at 3 points: the caller's `except Exception: pass`, the function's `except Exception: return response`, and the case where the repair dispatched and returned nothing runnable. Only the SUCCESS path spoke, so 3 different endings were indistinguishable in the record — and the measurement above was the only evidence the mitigation works, on runs whose repair could have quietly failed. All 3 now say so. 6 executing tests against a stubbed client with no network and no cost, 4 mutations, all caught.
`bench/experiment_11_orchestrator.py:1442` sets tools to none unconditionally for that route.

But maybe as an informative statistic only, since I don't think you are saying if measuring it should also change behaviour too?"* Built as `result["target_complexity"]` in `bench/reference_runner_v3.py`, carrying `gamma_input`, `beta`, `r_squared`, `n_windows`, `window_chars`, `target_tokens` and a plain-English `reading`, because the direction is counter-intuitive — **high gamma is simple and repetitive, low gamma is complex and novel**. This also closes the additive standard's own failure mode named in 4.2: `compute_gamma_input` was **imported by the live runner at `:221` and called nowhere**, an addition nothing reached. **A FALLBACK THAT LOOKED LIKE A MEASUREMENT NEARLY SHIPPED:** below `MIN_WINDOWS` the function returns an ASSUMED beta of 0.5, and at the default 10,000-character window every ordinary code target falls below it — `bench/dm/_memory.py` is 20,563 chars but only **1,485 tokens**, a 13.8:1 ratio against the module's assumed 4:1 — so the report would have carried `gamma_input` 0.5 in a field a reader takes as measured. Found by a test written to check the statistic's DIRECTION, which returned 0.5 for both a repetitive and a novel text. The window is now derived from the module's own tokeniser, aiming for 2 x `MIN_WINDOWS` because a 3-point fit returns `r_squared` 1.0000 by arithmetic rather than by evidence, and the record carries an explicit `fit: measured | ASSUMED_DEFAULT`. Measured: `_memory.py` gamma 0.394127 at r-squared 0.996892 over 7 windows. **PANEL ROUND 8 FOUND A THIRD NOT-MEASURED CASE, AND IT RECORDED 1.0 BESIDE PROSE SAYING 0.5 (cc2 and fable, convergent).** When a target tokenises to nothing, `compute_gamma_input` returns early at `input_complexity.py:211` with **gamma 1.0** and never reaches the assumed-default branch — so the flag read `ASSUMED_DEFAULT` while the field held the extreme *maximally simple* value and the reading said 0.5. Reachable, not theoretical: `tokenize` keeps only `[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*` runs longer than 2 characters, so any CJK, right-to-left, minified or short-identifier target yields 0 tokens. **Fixed** to 3 states — `measured` / `NO_TOKENS` / `ASSUMED_DEFAULT` — with the reading interpolating the actual gamma so prose cannot drift from the field again, and the `except` broadened to `Exception` (fable) because a `MemoryError` or `TypeError` would otherwise reach the outer handler, which returns **before `target_hashes` is recorded** — an informative statistic able to blind the integrity control, in a project where 35 of 39 archived runs already carry no target hash. **cc2 independently confirmed the `n_windows >= MIN_WINDOWS` key is correct**, deriving that `_fit_heaps` cannot reach its `(0,0,0)` sentinel at 3 or more windows. Cost measured: 41 ms on the 776 KB runner, 0.46 s on a synthetic 7.8 MB target, once per run. `bench/tests/test_target_complexity_is_reported_2026-09-10.py`, 10 tests.

Following from 4.2: the term that encodes simplicity in the model is a constant, and its measuring module is unreached. This is the additive standard's own failure mode sitting inside the mathematics.

**His question is the right one and it is NOT rhetorical.** Informative-only is trivial if nu is currently read by nothing that decides. It is NOT trivial if nu already feeds a live decision path as a constant, because then replacing a constant with a real measurement changes behaviour BY CONSTRUCTION, whether or not that was the intent. Which of those is true is being established from the code rather than the documentation; the answer determines whether this is a 1-line reporting addition or a change that must go through the project's shadow mechanism first. **SETTLED 2026-09-09 BY EXECUTION, and the answer is NO.** `nu_b` and `nu_f` are literal arguments to `check_sk_threshold_corrected`, the live fix-admission gate at `bench/reference_runner_v3.py:17131`. Calling it with everything else held fixed (s_k = 0.60, q = 0.5, R = 0.5): at the shipped nu of (0.05, 0.20) the threshold is 0.504931 and the verdict is **ADMISSIBLE**; at (0.10, 0.30) the threshold is 0.683292 and the verdict is **REJECTED**. SymPy confirms nu_eff is strictly increasing in both terms, so a measured complexity cannot leave the gate where it is — it can only move it. Across the reachable nu box, **570 of 676 grid points differ from the shipped verdict**, 84.3%, Wilson [81.4%, 86.9%], Clopper-Pearson [81.4%, 87.0%].

**Therefore informative-only is a CHOICE that must be built, not a default.** The measured complexity must be carried by a quantity the gate does not read — the candidate is `gamma_input` from the input-complexity module — or kept out of `entry["model_params"]` entirely. Putting it into nu changes which fixes are admitted and stops archived runs replaying, which is the same cost the founder knowingly accepted for the corrected threshold on 2026-09-06. **His instinct in asking was right; the question was not rhetorical.**

**THE TOKEN IS ACTUALLY ROTATED, 2026-09-19 20:00 BST, and this entry moves from COMMITTED to ENABLED because until today it described instructions rather than a rotation.** The old token, 60 characters starting `ievd`, had been in `.env` since 2026-08-16, 34 days. The new one starts `Bu30`; `scripts/zenodo_token_check.py --live` returns HTTP 200 with 1 deposition visible, which is the CDSFL experimental archive. The other 9 credentials in that file are byte-identical either side of the change, proved by the digest `567852245d5e8cf0...` printed before and after.

**Doing it rather than describing it found 2 defects.** First, `.env` carries the macOS `uchg` immutable flag, `shutil.copy2` copies that flag to the backup, and `os.chmod` on an immutable file raises EPERM -- so the first attempt died AFTER the founder had pasted a token Zenodo displays exactly once. The tool now handles the flag and, more importantly, does every step that can fail BEFORE it asks for the secret. Second, `zenodo_token_check.py` read only the first 2,000 bytes of a 3,718-byte reply, parsed the truncated JSON, and reported the resulting error as *"could not reach zenodo.org"* -- an instrument truncating its own evidence and calling the truncation an outage, on a run where the server answered 200 and the token was valid. It now reads the whole body and distinguishes rejected, unreachable and unparseable, because those 3 call for 3 different actions.

20 tests in `bench/tests/test_zenodo_rotate_2026-09-19.py`. Restoring the 2,000-byte truncation fails the regression test; making the tool print the token fails the leak test; both run and reverted.

**DONE 2026-09-11, and the fix is Python's own scoping rule rather than a heuristic.** The guard collected tuple-returning function NAMES across the whole repository and flagged any binding of such a name that was later tested for truth, without resolving which function was called — so a new script defining `scan()` returning a 3-tuple took `scripts/supersession_check.py:149` red for `if not findings:`, a truth test that is entirely correct because THAT file's own `scan()` returns a LIST. **A file that DEFINES a name shadows every other definition of it**, so `_locally_shadowed()` removes from the flagged set, for that file only, any name the file defines whose local definition demonstrably does not return a tuple of 2 or more elements. **The guard is not weakened and there is a test for each direction:** a file whose OWN function returns a tuple is still flagged, and an IMPORTED verdict function is still flagged — which is the defect the guard was built for, `scripts/cdsfl_seal_logs.py` binding a verdict whole and testing it. 2 mutations verified red, including the over-correction that shadows everything a file defines. **The workaround is now unnecessary:** the new function was renamed `attempts()` to dodge the collision, which removed the symptom and left the cause. **A false positive here is not a harmless annoyance** — "the suite went red for a file nobody touched" is how a guard's output starts being ignored, which is this project's own sentence about 3 different alarms.

The entry's CURRENT evidence files are copied into that old tree and run there, so today's test meets yesterday's code, which is exactly the question V9 asks. **All 114 DONE entries are checkable:** every one names an existing test file and every one's closing commit is locatable, 114 of 114, Wilson [96.7401%, 100.0000%]. **MEASURED on a reproducible sample of 24** by `scripts/does_the_evidence_go_red_2026-10-17.py`: **17 DISCRIMINATES, 2 DECORATIVE, 5 INCONCLUSIVE.** So **2 of 19 decided = 10.5263% decorative, Wilson [2.9359%, 31.3941%], Clopper-Pearson [1.3012%, 33.1377%]** — roughly 1 DONE entry in 10 rests on evidence that would have stayed green with its own fix absent. **THE 2 ARE NAMED, because a rate with no members is not actionable.** **A11:** 27 of 27 tests pass at the parent commit, so it discriminates nothing. **R2:** 4 passed and **14 SKIPPED** — a test that skips when its subject is absent is always green, which is the most deceptive form because it reads as a pass. Both pass today, which is why the defect was invisible until the evidence was run against a tree WITHOUT the fix. **Repairing those 2 is separate work and is not claimed here.** **A THIRD OUTCOME EXISTS AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THE FIGURE HONEST.** 5 of the 24 are INCONCLUSIVE: the evidence cannot be COLLECTED at the parent commit, because the module it imports did not exist yet. That is not discrimination, it is the test failing to run, and counting it as a pass for V9 would repeat the error this project recorded when a crashed check was read as a passing one. They are excluded from the denominator and reported separately. **CHECKING ALL 114 ENTRIES IS NOT DONE AT COMMIT TIME**, because it costs a git worktree and a pytest invocation per entry and his machine is a fixed resource. **B29. `sv` measures memory against the previous save, so it refuses the follow-up that fixes the previous save's own postcondition.** Added 2026-10-17T23:06:48+01:00. **WHAT HAPPENED TONIGHT, TWICE OVER.** `scripts/cdsfl_sv.py` committed and pushed at `2944e376`, then FAILED its own postcondition: the newest `SESSION STATE` block in `resources/RECOVERY.md` was 70 commits behind HEAD against a ceiling of 60. That failure is BY DESIGN -- sv deliberately preserves that block and will not write it -- so the remedy is to write the block and re-run sv. On the re-run the `memory-updated` check refused the save, because its baseline is `_previous_sv_commit`, which is now `2944e376` itself, and this session's memory was written 11 seconds BEFORE that commit. **The gate therefore refuses a save for lacking memory that exists**, and the only route through is to write more memory or to reach for `--allow-incomplete-save`, which the script's own alert tells the operator not to do. **MEASURED, AND MY FIRST FIGURE OVERSTATED IT.** Across all history 117 of 209 consecutive sv pairs fall within 6 hours, but the `memory-updated` check did not exist for most of them: it entered in `ddd6e4c3` on 2026-08-06. Restricting to pairs whose second commit postdates the check leaves 83, of which **14 are follow-ups inside 15 minutes -- 15.7303%, Wilson [9.6078%, 24.6888%]** (re-derived 2026-10-29; the denominator has grown from 83 to 89 as saves landed, so the earlier 16.8675% was stale rather than wrong) -- and 7 of those 14 subjects name the session-state block, the A23 guard or a missing producer citation explicitly (8 was wrong: the classifier in `scripts/do_options_three_and_one_compose_2026-10-29.py` and an independent hand count of all 14 subjects both give 7), which is this exact postcondition. So the shape has recurred 14 times in 72 days and is not tonight's accident. Producer: `scripts/how_often_is_a_second_sv_refused_2026-10-17.py`. **WHAT THE CHECK IS FOR, AND WHY THE BASELINE IS THE DEFECT RATHER THAN THE CHECK.** Its stated purpose is sound and should not be weakened: *"an sv that commits code and documents but leaves the persistent-memory folder untouched saves the work and loses the session."* The defect is that it infers "this session's memory" from "newer than the last sv commit". That inference is correct for the FIRST save of a session and wrong for every follow-up, because a follow-up's own predecessor is the save whose memory it is being asked to produce again. **THE RECOMMENDED FIX, which is additive rather than a loosening.** Have sv RECORD whether its postconditions passed, and have the `memory-updated` baseline skip back to the last sv that recorded a clean finish. That replaces an inference with a committed fact, keeps the guarantee exactly as strong for a first save, and costs one recorded field. The alternative of special-casing a short time window is rejected: a 15-minute gap is also what two genuinely separate pieces of work look like when one follows the other quickly, so time cannot distinguish them and the distinction being drawn is completeness, not recency. **WHY THIS IS NOT BEING BUILT WITHOUT HIM.** It changes when a save gate PASSES, and his standing pattern is that loosening a gate's effect is his call even when the repair is a correctness repair -- the guard that refuses to move a finding labelled mathematical onto the path where code is checked took exactly this route on 2026-10-16 and he ruled it. The script's own alert does grant standing permission here (*"If a check fired on a save you know IS complete, the CHECK is the defect -- repair it in `scripts/cdsfl_sv.py` rather than reaching for the override again"*, his RULING 4 of 2026-08-06), so this is a narrow yes/no rather than an open design question. **FOR DONE:** his word, then the recorded-completion field, the baseline change, and a guard that executes both the first-save and follow-save paths rather than reading them. **NEEDS HIS RULING.** **HIS RULING, 2026-10-19:** *"Verdict: Option 3. Dut do Options 3 and 1 compose, if an event occurs where a save operation does not complete cleanly?"* (*Dut* is *But*.) **RUN THE STALENESS CHECK BEFORE INVOKING sv**, which is option 3 and is now standing practice. **★ HIS COMPOSITION QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THIS ENTRY'S CLAIM THAT IT ALREADY WAS IS WITHDRAWN, 2026-10-29.** The sentence above read that the question *"is answered in the session note of 2026-10-20 and is not a decision he owes"*. **THERE IS NO SUCH NOTE.** 21 tracked files carry that date in their names, but exactly 1 of them is a session note -- `experimental_notes/Panel_Joint_What_Breaks_The_Capability_Tie_2026-10-20_FULL_RECORD.md` -- and it is about a capability tie, not about sv. **None of the 21 mentions B29 at all**, the session note included. So the justifying p = 1.6e-7 is already superseded in the committed record. **WHAT IS NEW HERE IS THE COST, and it falsifies 1 sentence of that producer**, which reads *"The interventional test is cheap, because both seats are free."* Free of money is not cheap: the rate the simultaneously-dispatched condition must reproduce is **1 of 68 rounds, 1.4706%, Wilson [0.2601%, 7.8710%]**, which needs **47 rounds for 50% power and 109 rounds for 80% power** -- at 2 seats and 12 to 29 minutes a seat, **18.8 to 45.4 hours and 43.6 to 105.4 hours of his Max quota**. At 1 round in each condition, P(0 events given serialisation cures nothing) = **0.9559**, so a clean serialised arm is the likely outcome whether or not anything was cured, and the best possible 2 by 2 at 1 round each gives Fisher one-sided **p = 0.5000**. The committed producer measures the overshoot as a share of the cap, +8.68% of 1800 seconds rather than 156 seconds absolute, which is the better instrument, because a subprocess killed at a deadline overshoots by its own teardown cost and that cost scales with the deadline. Chasing that contradiction produced this measurement, and the paragraph is restored. **THE CAUSE: `scripts/note_vagueness_lint.py` IS PATH-SENSITIVE.** `NOTE_STANDARD_STAMP` fires only for a file under a directory named `experimental_notes`. Measured on identical bytes across 6 notes: the real path and a `/tmp/<x>/experimental_notes/` copy agree every time, while a flat `/tmp/<x>/` copy and an `after_`-prefixed copy lose a finding in **4 of 6**, and in every case the lost finding is `MISSING NOTE STANDARD STAMP`. **AND THE PRE-COMMIT SHARES THE BLIND SPOT.** `hooks/pre-commit:375-392` materialises both sides into a FLAT `mktemp -d` directory — `git show ":$f" > "$STAGED_COPY/after_$base"` and `git show "HEAD:$f" > "$STAGED_COPY/before_$base"` — so the `experimental_notes` parent is gone from both and the stamp rule fires on neither. **THAT MAKES IT A SOUND RATCHET AND AN INCOMPLETE DETECTOR**, and the distinction matters: blind on BOTH sides, it can never report a change that is not there, so it cannot produce the false +1 CC1's mixed-path check produced. Its job is "this commit must not make it worse" and it does that faithfully for every rule it can see. What it cannot do is notice a note delivered with a missing or stale standard stamp, which is precisely what the foot-line convention exists to catch. **CC1's OWN CHECK WAS THE WORSE INSTRUMENT**: the hook is consistently blind, whereas CC1 compared a `/tmp` baseline against a REAL path so one side saw the rule and the other did not, and an earlier run of the same check used a baseline captured before an intervening commit. **WHAT SLIPPED PAST, BOUNDED CAREFULLY.** Of 522 notes in `experimental_notes/`, 196 name no standard at all and 161 name only an older one. **The 161 are NOT defects** — the convention states that notes written under earlier versions retain their version-specific foot-lines, so reporting "357 of 522 non-compliant" would have been wrong. Splitting the 196 by the date in the filename against v1's lock date of 2026-04-21: 121 legitimately predate the standard, 2 carry no date, and **73 postdate it and name none — 13.9847% of all 522, Wilson [11.2717%, 17.2238%], Clopper-Pearson [11.1245%, 17.2598%]**. The newest are `WORK_IN_FLIGHT_2026-10-07.md`, `Proposal_Fingerprint_Falsification_Dimension_2026-10-05.md` and `WORK_IN_PROGRESS_2026-10-04.md`. **73 is an UPPER BOUND on genuine violations**, because several are working scratch files rather than delivered notes, and the standard governs delivered notes and TTS. **For DONE:** make the hook preserve the parent directory when it materialises both sides — writing to `$STAGED_COPY/after/experimental_notes/<base>` and `$STAGED_COPY/before/experimental_notes/<base>` keeps the ratchet's blind-on-both-sides soundness while letting it see path-sensitive rules — then re-run it over the 73 and either stamp them or record why each is exempt. The local memory-budget hook cannot tell an instruction from a prohibition, and its false positives select for less-safe briefs.** Added 2026-10-17T01:20:36+01:00. **OBSERVED TWICE in one turn on 2026-10-17.** `~/.claude/hooks/local_resource_budget.py:98` computes `wants_pytest = bool(re.search(r"\bpytest\b|python3? -m pytest|full board|the suite\b", low))` over the whole prompt text and refuses the call when it also fans out to several agents. The match is **polarity-blind**: a delegated brief whose text says *do not* invoke the verification tooling matches on the very words that express the prohibition. The first refusal fired on an explicit *"do NOT run pytest"*; the second, after that word was removed, fired on the phrase *"cost more than a full board run"* inside the same prohibition. **WHY THIS IS ABOVE THRESHOLD RATHER THAN AN ANNOYANCE.** The guard exists because 263 delegated verification runs cost 4,557.8 s against 3,998.65 s for 1 whole-board pass, measured 2026-10-11. But an author who cannot state the limit in the brief has 2 remaining options: drop the limit from the brief, or rephrase around the matcher. Both weaken the brief, and the first is actively dangerous because a delegated agent with no stated limit is more likely to invoke the tooling, not less. **So the guard's false positive pushes authors toward the exact behaviour the guard exists to prevent.** This is the same defect class as `execute-do-not-grep`: a text matcher standing in for a judgement about intent. **FOR DONE:** require an imperative or infinitival context before refusing — match forms such as `run pytest`, `invoke pytest`, `python3 -m pytest` — and suppress the match where a negation appears within a short window before it. Guard it with a test that CALLS the hook's predicate over both polarities and requires the prohibition to pass and the instruction to be refused, per `execute-do-not-grep`. **NEEDS NO RULING:** the guard keeps its purpose and gains precision, so this is additive under the additive standard.

**ANSWERED 2026-10-17 17:21 BST, WITH A MECHANISM RATHER THAN A RULE: YES, AND HERE IS HOW.** His question was *"Then can similar errors be prevented in the futre [future]?"* The 7 withdrawn statements fall into **3 counting shapes**, not 7 separate mistakes: **(1) DOUBLE MATCHING** — *"the producing script matched every run log under 2 patterns at once"*; **(2) LINES REPORTED AS OCCURRENCES** — *"counted lines containing a match and reported them as occurrences"*; **(3) SELF-INCLUSION** — a census that *"included the 3 documents written about the term it was counting"*.

**ALL 3 RECURRED ON 2026-10-17, which is the evidence that a rule was not enough.** A detector read its OWN SOURCE as live code and reported 5 defects, every one a line of its own docstring. Another read its own explanatory comment as the code it was checking. A substring scan reported **190** hits for "promot" — this project's own shadow PROMOTION — **64** for "division", mostly arithmetic, and **25** for "fixture", which is pytest. Each was caught by accident, not by a mechanism.

**`bench/counting.py` MAKES THE 3 SHAPES HARD TO WRITE.** `occurrences` and `lines_containing` put the unit in the FUNCTION NAME; `count_over` takes `unit` as KEYWORD-ONLY WITH NO DEFAULT and excludes the CALLING FILE by default, REPORTING what it excluded; `overlapping_patterns` returns both a distinct total and a sum, so a sum exceeding the distinct total is itself the evidence of double counting. **The margins are measured, not rhetorical:** on one line holding a term 3 times the 2 unit functions differ by **3x**, and on a probe whose own source mentions its term 8 times, self-inclusion inflates a total from **3 to 11 — a factor of 3.67**.

**WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO.** It cannot stop a producer choosing the wrong population; nothing can. The claim is narrower and testable: the 3 shapes that cost 7 claims are now hard to write, and both mutations — self-exclusion defaulted off, and `occurrences` counting lines — go red.

**ONE HONEST LIMIT.** `count_over` was written first with `unit` DEFAULTED, which made its own docstring's claim that the unit was required FALSE — the same description-versus-behaviour shape as every other defect here. It is now keyword-only with no default.

A fallback is the path a config object WITHOUT the field takes, so leaving them at False would have let a stub config keep the superseded behaviour silently — the silent-defaulting class this project keeps finding. `HARDENED_GATE_DEFAULT` is now the only expression, and a test parses the runner to fail if a second one appears. **WHAT CHANGES, STATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, because this is a behaviour change and not a threshold move.** The gate becomes the CONJUNCTION of a sustained, leave-one-round-out-robust critical gamma and N consecutive settled rounds carrying no novel critical, computed on the settled post-reconciliation registry; the legacy gamma-alt path is bypassed and all-novelty gamma is kept as a diagnostic. It is NOT simply stricter, so the evidence that it converges rather than stalling matters: **all 3 shakedown legs ran with it ON and converged at rounds 3, 4 and 4, each reaching 1.000 on the decay curve.** **AN EXPLICIT `False` IS STILL HONOURED**, and a test pins that: his ruling sets the default, and an experiment reproducing an archived run must still be able to select the legacy gate, or replay becomes impossible — a cost he did not agree to. **GUARD:** 7 tests, 3 of 3 mutations caught. **And one of them was vacuous at first:** it compared the field's default to the constant with `is`, and since both are `True` and `True` is a singleton, writing the field as a bare literal left all 7 green. Whether a rule has one expression is a property of the SOURCE, so that test now parses the runner, while the behaviour stays covered by the runtime tests beside it.

**ANSWERED 2026-10-17 17:21 BST, AND THE EVIDENCE DISAGREES WITH HIS PARENTHETICAL FOR THESE RUNS.** His question: *"If this is on (and it probably should be), what effect would it have on our experiments? ... human review is always part of the system anyway ... Where does this switch fit into this?"*

**HIS PREMISE IS RIGHT AND THE SWITCH IS NOT AT THOSE BOUNDARIES.** His review is at the ENDS — he picks the target, he reads the output. Read from its call sites, `hil_review` inserts a pause BETWEEN ROUNDS: in monolithic mode after EVERY round, in burst mode at each phase boundary, and **both sites `sys.exit(42)`** after writing a partial report and setting `hil_status = "paused_for_review"`. **So it is a PAUSE, not a review step** — nothing is shown to him that the final report does not already carry; what changes is WHEN, and that the run stops until he acts.

**THE EFFECT.** Turning it on converts 1 autonomous run into N sequential sessions, 1 per round. Leg 3 ran **5 rounds in 71.5 minutes**, so 5 stops, each needing his attention and a resume. The larger consequence is that **intervening between rounds changes what the experiment MEASURES**: the rounds after an intervention are not the same process as the rounds before it, so a convergence figure spanning one is not a measurement of AUTONOMOUS convergence — which is this programme's success criterion, 3 consecutive clean convergences on the prose target.

**SO: NOT ON FOR THESE RUNS, AND ON FOR A RUN MEANT TO STEER.** That disagrees with *"it probably should be"* for the programme now in flight, and agrees with it for any run whose purpose is to steer rather than to measure. The choice is now a choice rather than a default.

**MEASURED, so "never been on" is a figure:** **0 of 47** shipped configs set `hil_review` at all — 0.0000%, Wilson [0.0000%, 7.5558%], Clopper-Pearson [0.0000%, 7.5486%] — and **0 archived run reports** carry `hil_status` or `hil_paused_at_round`. The **54 `.py` and 28 `.json`** files under `bench/logs/` that mention those keys are sandbox-harvest COPIES OF THE RUNNER SOURCE. **Counting them would have reported 82 pauses where there were none** — exactly the self-inclusion shape task C2 now guards against, and the producer draws the distinction explicitly.

If so this is the option you should implement."* **RECOVERED**, from `experimental_notes/What_Was_Actually_Implemented_2026-10-11.md` under the heading *Item 8 recovered*: the better way was **incremental stream-json parsing**. **VERIFIED RATHER THAN RESTATED, and it dominates on a named property**, which is what the additive standard requires before choosing between 2 mechanisms. A **completion marker** separates *printed* from *not printed*, and a DEAD seat never prints it either — so it cannot tell finished from died. **The clock separates nothing:** measured by `scripts/the_cap_was_measured_on_censored_data_2026-10-08.py`, a degraded attempt issued **88 tool calls at 20.455 s per call and never converged**, a healthy one **converged in 49 at 20.816 s per call**, and a third seat ran at 15.024 s per call — a spread of **5.792 s** across all 3. The RATE is stable whether a seat is working or churning; only the COUNT differs, so a longer clock buys churn, which is why the dispatcher's record of a 3600 s raise reverted within the hour stands. **A live call count separates all 3 states** — working, churning, dead. **AND WHY IT HAD TO BE BUILT BEFORE THE CAP COULD STOP BEING ARBITRARY.** All **135** archived per-attempt records carry a total count and a total elapsed, and **not one carries a time per call**, so the inter-call gap distribution — the only thing a non-arbitrary stall bound can be derived from — is unmeasurable today. A count threshold alone would not do it either: the 2 attempts killed at the cap had **78 and 89** calls, both below the 90th percentile of 95, so they were killed by TIME at a normal call count. This change produces the missing data; the derived bound is the second step and is NOT claimed as done. **WHAT IS BUILT.** `_run_cli_incrementally` consumes the CLI's stdout as it arrives, so (1) the tool-call count is observable **mid-flight** and logged every 10th call, where before no progress signal existed at all; (2) **partial output survives a timeout** — `subprocess.run(capture_output=True)` discards everything when it raises and the old handler never read `e.output`, which is the recorded **"1800 s for 0 words"**; and (3) every call is **stamped with its arrival time**. **STRICTLY ADDITIVE.** It runs only where a tool-log sink is set, which is already the only place the CLI is asked for stream-json, so the text path keeps `subprocess.run` untouched and a dispatch without a sink behaves exactly as before — pinned by a test that parses the dispatcher to require both calls present. The timeout still raises the same exception type, so the retry path is unchanged. **ONE PARSING RULE, NOT TWO.** The per-line parse was factored out of `_parse_stream_json` so the incremental reader and the whole-capture parser cannot drift — the shape the note linter's own `paragraphs()` records breaking an exemption set. The caller then compares the 2 counts over the same bytes and REPORTS a disagreement rather than silently preferring one. **GUARDS:** 9 tests, 5 of 5 mutations caught — dropping the partial output from the timeout, removing the timestamps, never calling the progress hook, letting a hook exception kill a dispatch, and re-spelling the per-line rule (which fails 7 of 9). **AND 2 DEFECTS OF MINE WERE FOUND WHILE DOING IT.** My earlier counter refactor left an **unreachable `return len(blocking)`** after the real return, referring to a name that no longer exists in that scope — dead, and it would have raised `NameError` had anything reached it. And `test_a_deferred_critical_can_stop_blocking_A4_eventually` was asserting on the SOURCE TEXT of `unverified_critical_count`, searching for a string the refactor had moved into `blocking_entry_ids`; the behaviour never changed, but a source-text test cannot tell a behaviour change from a rename. It now builds a registry, marks a critical exhausted, and requires the counter to stop counting it — and requires the sibling routing reader to agree, since one predicate was the point. Disabling the valve turns it red.

The clock WAS captured in the same step, and the value was still typed from memory rather than read from what came back, which is the only way this fault happens. Recording it once plainly did not prevent it, so what has to change is the order of operations: capture the clock, read the value that comes back, then compose the text. **OBSERVED, NOT REASONED ABOUT.** On the C24/C25 commit and again on the C27 commit the gate printed, 4 times each, that `experimental_notes/CDSFL_MASTER_TASK_LIST.md` *"is partially staged AND the repair collides with a hunk you left out. NOT staged: staging it would commit work you withheld."* **No work had been withheld on either commit:** both were staged with `git add -A`. The citation repair therefore lagged a commit behind twice, and each time needed a separate follow-up commit to land. **THE CAUSE.** `cdsfl_is_partially_staged` asks whether a path has both staged and unstaged changes, and it is evaluated **after** the stage-0 repairs have written. A fully staged file that a repair has just touched satisfies that test by construction. It has no snapshot copy — the snapshot is taken before any repair writes, and copies only paths that were partially staged **then** — so `cdsfl_stage_repair_delta` cannot compute a delta, returns 1, and the caller reports a collision that did not occur. **THIS IS THE THIRD DISTINCT CAUSE OF A FALSE COLLISION MESSAGE IN THAT ONE BRANCH.** The helper's own comments record the first two: a path containing a space was word-split and never snapshotted, and a repair that changed nothing produced an empty patch that returned the collision code. Each was fixed where it was found. The branch kept crying wolf because the predicate was **re-derived after the fact** rather than read from the one record that cannot drift. **FIXED** by keying the branch on the snapshot: the delta mechanism runs only where a snapshot copy exists, which is exactly the set of paths the author partially staged **before** anything wrote. Everywhere else a plain `git add` is used, and it is safe there by construction, because nothing was withheld to sweep. **WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE NOISE.** A guard that cries wolf on the ordinary case is one an operator learns to wave through — the pattern this project already recorded once in the containment alarm — and the failure mode here is silent: had the follow-up commit been forgotten, the stale citations would have shipped while the working tree looked correct. That is the 2026-09-11 defect, found then only by cloning HEAD. **GUARD:** 3 tests in a new class in `bench/tests/test_precommit_restages_repairs_2026-09-11.py` reproducing the exact scenario — fully stage with no withheld hunk, let a repair write, then re-stage — asserting the repair reaches the index, that no collision is reported, and that the plain add is used rather than the delta path. Reverting the condition fails all 3. 47 tests in the 2 commit-gate files.

Its own comment records the consequence, measured 2026-09-02: *"2 of 2,050 archived findings are recorded as raised by more than one model, because when two models find one defect the runner mints two unlinked canonicals and the second is merged away."* **AND I DO NOT RECOMMEND APPLYING IT, which is the opposite of the agreeable answer.** Measured across 61 runs and **2,954** described findings using the harness's **own** `_routing_similarity`, so the judgement is the system's rather than mine: **33 pairs** reach the 0.85 threshold the routing ladder actually uses. **But only 6 of the 33 carry substantial descriptions on both sides.** 6 are fragments of 8 distinct words or fewer and 21 are mid-length, where word overlap reaches 0.85 on shared code tokens such as `finding_id: str` without the findings being the same defect at all. Reading the 6 substantial pairs, several are findings **about** other findings — *"Addresses C0007"*, *"VERDICT: CONFIRM C0014"* — which are legitimately distinct. **MY OWN FIRST FIGURE IS WITHDRAWN IN THE SAME BREATH.** The script initially reported 33 pairs and **66 of 2,954 findings involved, 2.2343%, Wilson [1.7601%, 2.8325%]**, and recommended putting the change to him. That is the over-merge direction, which this project has already measured as the more damaging one: it hides the open item behind the closed one, and the ticket register's own integrity check exists because 3 settled tickets once concealed 5 open task entries. **WHAT THE 2 REGISTERS LEGITIMATELY DIFFER ON, which is the useful part of the answer.** A task entry has an external, stable reference to key on and is written once by one author. A finding has neither: it is minted by a model mid-run and its description is whatever that model wrote, so a counter is an honest label for it. **The principle that transferred was never the hash** — it was that a lookup happens before a new identity is minted, and that needs a signal reliable enough to act on. THE LIMIT ON TICKETS CARRYING NO IDENTITY IS IRREVERSIBLE ONCE BREACHED, AND I BREACHED IT: 3 TICKETS I RAISED BY HAND TOOK THE COUNT FROM 317 TO 320 AND NO AVAILABLE REMEDY LOWERS IT.** Added 2026-10-29T08:13:53+00:00. **HOW IT WAS FOUND.** `bench/tests/test_an_identity_is_derived_not_remembered_2026-10-28.py::test_the_identityless_count_does_not_grow` is red in the full suite of 2026-10-29, and it is CORRECT to be red. **320 of 2,887 tickets carry neither a `task_ref` nor an `anchor`**, 0.110842 with a 95% Wilson interval of [0.099903, 0.122814] agreed to 6 decimal places by statsmodels and an independent NumPy closed form against a ceiling of 317 measured at 2026-10-28T02:10:18Z. The 3 additions are `qs:7d558a3e3381`, `pf:b4517f6ecfe6` and `pf:b0d8ca44a450`, all OPEN, all `source=chat`, all created by me between 04:05 and 06:06 on 2026-10-29. **THIS IS THE DOCUMENTED MISTAKE REPEATED.** The escape hatch is `TicketStore.propose_from_chat`, which DERIVES the anchor as `chat#<clock>#<8 hex of the text>`; its own docstring records that on 2026-10-27 5 questions were raised by hand, all 5 came out identityless, 4 had to be re-raised, and that *"the escape hatch `_distinct` provides was designed, documented and simply not used"*. I then did not use it either. **THE 320 CANNOT BE REDUCED, AND THIS IS EXECUTED RATHER THAN ARGUED.** Against a scratch copy of `bench/tickets/tickets.jsonl`: baseline **320**, raise 1 identityless ticket → **321**, call `migrate_identity` onto a tid derived from a proper anchor → **322**, raise the same item correctly through `propose_from_chat` → **322**. It never returned even to the breached level, let alone below it, because a correct re-raise ADDS an anchored record while the bare tombstone stays. The cause is structural and deliberate: `migrate_identity` preserves history by keeping the old record as a `MERGED` tombstone, and that tombstone is itself identityless, so every history-preserving remedy ADDS a bare record. **287 of the 320 are exactly such tombstones**, left by the 2026-10-17 identity migration. **A SECOND DEFECT FOUND IN THE SAME PROBE, AND IT IS INDEPENDENT OF THE RATCHET.** `migrate_identity` copies every field with `asdict(old)` and replaces only `tid`, so migrating onto a tid DERIVED from an anchor produces a record whose `anchor` is still `''` — measured: `moved.anchor == ''` while its tid was computed from `chat#...`. **B63. THE STOP GATE CREDITS FOLLOW ONLY FOR THE FIRST FFAFP CYCLE IN A TURN, SO IN A LONG AUTONOMOUS TURN IT CANNOT BE SATISFIED AFTER THE FIRST EDIT.**
<!-- task: B63 | state: DONE | status: COMMITTED | evidence: bench/tests/test_the_follow_window_is_per_cycle_2026-11-01.py | ruled: 2026-11-01 -->

**NEEDS HIS RULING: whether to anchor the evidence window per FFAFP cycle rather than per turn.** It is his because it changes a gate that holds this session to its own discipline, and loosening such a gate unattended is the one move this project's record says to make slowly. **RECOMMENDATION: anchor it per cycle.** That is the SIMPLEST SUFFICIENT fix, because it moves 1 window boundary and nothing else, and it is ADDITIVE, because the gate keeps every step it checks today and gains the ability to be satisfied more than once in a turn. **NO COMPOSABILITY CLAIM IS MADE**, because no second repair was measured to improve on it. Added to the entry 2026-11-01 so the entry and its authored detail agree: the detail said this was his while the entry asked nothing, and 2 surfaces disagreeing is what lets a question go missing.

Added 2026-11-01T04:05. **★ THIS ENTRY REPLACES 2 WRONG DIAGNOSES OF MINE, BOTH REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT WITHIN 20 MINUTES, AND THE GATE WAS RIGHT ABOUT ME ALL ALONG.**

**WHAT WAS OBSERVED.** The gate refused 4 times in succession for a missing FOLLOW, always naming the same files, on turns that each ran a `grep -r` naming every changed file's basename and then ran failable tests. Nothing done in the current turn could clear it.

**MY FIRST DIAGNOSIS, WITHDRAWN: an undersized scan window latching a stale turn.** I claimed `TAIL_BYTES` at 8 MiB against a 638 MB transcript left 0 turn-close boundaries in the window. **REFUTED by its own measurement:** across 35,111 inter-turn gaps the LARGEST is 1,605,379 bytes, **0 exceed the window**, and the last turn-opening sits 5,732 bytes from the end of the file. The window was never too small. **★ THOSE 3 NUMBERS CARRY NO PRODUCER AND MAY NOT BE REQUOTED, found 2026-11-01 while citing them to him.** `measure()` in `scripts/follow_is_credited_only_before_the_first_edit_2026-11-01.py` computes the window, the scans and the first mutation; it computes NO inter-turn gaps, so 35,111 and 1,605,379 exist only as prose in that docstring and in this paragraph. They are also not reproducible in principle: they measure one growing transcript at one instant, so a producer run later would answer a different question. **The CLAIM they support IS reproducible and is what survives** -- that the byte window is not the cause -- because `scripts/follow_is_credited_only_before_the_first_edit_2026-11-01.py` reports the window, the transcript size and the turn-closes it finds on whatever transcript it is pointed at. They were withdrawn from `experimental_notes/Decisions_Awaiting_You_2026-11-01.txt` before he read them, and the z3 and SymPy proof that replaced them reproduces on demand.

**MY SECOND DIAGNOSIS, ALSO WITHDRAWN: that an open turn being audited was a bug.** It is not. `ffafp_audit.scan` closes a turn only on `is_human_prompt`, which is correct — and the latched turn, timestamped 2026-11-01T02:01:40.342Z, IS the current turn, opened by the founder's own last message. The gate was auditing exactly the right turn.

**THE TRUE CAUSE, AND IT MAKES THE GATE'S VERDICT LITERALLY TRUE.** `ffafp_audit` line 889 builds the FOLLOW evidence as `scan_text = " ".join(t for i, t in scans if first is None or i < first)`, where `first` is `first_mut`, the index of the turn's FIRST mutation. Measured on the live turn: **`first_mut` is 2**, because the 2nd tool call after his message was a write to `resources/RECOVERY.md`; the turn holds **262 tool calls and 26 tree scans**, and **0 of the 26 fall before the first edit while all 26 fall after**. So `scan_text` is empty and `followed` is False. The gate was reporting a real miss: in this turn I edited before I traced, and every later scan is excluded BY DESIGN, which the code states in its own words — *"FOLLOW. A TREE SCAN naming the changed file or its stem, before the edit."*

**SO THE FINDING IS A DESIGN LIMITATION, NOT A DEFECT, AND IT IS WORTH HIS ATTENTION ANYWAY.** `first_mut` is set ONCE PER TURN. A supervised session is roughly one FFAFP cycle per turn, which is the shape the audit models. An autonomous overnight run is not: this single turn ran 262 tool calls across dozens of complete cycles. After the first edit the FOLLOW signal is unsatisfiable for the remainder of the turn, so a refusal can no longer distinguish *"never followed"* from *"followed 26 times, none of them before edit 1"*. **The gate's own reported figure — FOLLOW missing in 26 of the last 40 work turns — therefore cannot be read as 26 undisciplined turns, and should not be quoted as one until this is settled.**

**WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED.** That the discipline is wrong, or that the cutoff is wrong for a normal turn. Before an edit is exactly when a trace is worth something, and that is the whole point of FOLLOW.

**CANDIDATE REPAIRS, HIS CHOICE, NONE APPLIED.** (1) Account per MUTATION rather than per turn: credit a scan that names the file and precedes THAT file's first mutation, so each cycle is judged on its own. (2) Reset `first_mut` at a cycle boundary, which needs a boundary definition the transcript does not currently carry. (3) Leave it and accept that long autonomous turns report a standing FOLLOW miss, documenting that the figure is not a turn count. **My recommendation is 1**, because it measures the property the directive actually states — a trace before the change it relates to — rather than a property of turn packaging, and it needs no new concept. All 3 change when the gate refuses, which is his ruling of 2026-10-24, so this is **HIS DECISION**.

**★ CONFIRMED BY THE GATE'S OWN BEHAVIOUR, NOT ONLY BY READING ITS CODE, 2026-11-01 04:20.** A natural experiment settled it: in one turn the gate flagged FOLLOW **and** P-PASS; a failable test was then run and the very next refusal flagged **FOLLOW ALONE**. So P-PASS is satisfiable late in a turn and FOLLOW is not, which is exactly what the 2 predicates say — and the asymmetry is a single word.

| step | predicate | anchored on | satisfiable later in the turn |
|---|---|---|---|
| P-PASS | `verified_after = last is not None and any(i > last for i in failable_idx)` (`ffafp_audit.py:851`) | **`last`** mutation | **YES** — it tracks the most recent edit |
| FOLLOW | `scan_text = " ".join(t for i, t in scans if first is None or i < first)` (`:889`) | **`first`** mutation | **NO** — the window shuts at the first edit and never reopens |

**THAT MAKES THE REPAIR CONCRETE AND ALMOST SYMMETRIC WITH WORKING CODE ALREADY IN THE SAME FILE.** P-PASS already solves the equivalent problem by anchoring on the LAST mutation rather than the first, so FOLLOW can be given the same shape: credit a scan that names a file and precedes **that file's own** first mutation, which is the per-mutation accounting recommended above, with anchoring on `last` as the cruder fallback. **Neither is applied** — both change when the gate refuses, which is his ruling of 2026-10-24.

**★ A SECOND CONCRETE INSTANCE, FOUND THE SAME NIGHT AND CHEAPER TO FIX.** P-PASS is keyed on `last` — `verified_after = last is not None and any(i > last for i in failable_idx)` — and a MUTATION HARNESS WRITES THE SUBJECT BACK WHEN IT FINISHES. That restore is itself a mutation, so it becomes the turn's `last`, and a harness that ends by restoring leaves P-PASS unsatisfied however many tests it ran inside the sweep. Observed twice tonight: after `scripts/the_parked_presentation_mutations_2026-11-01.py` and again after the sweep that checks a comment against its default, each of which ran pytest 3 to 5 times internally. **The fix is 1 line in the harness, not a change to the gate:** run a failable check AFTER the final restore, so the trace lands on the right side of `last`. Both harnesses should do this, and the gate is correct to ask.

**★ A THIRD INSTANCE, AND THE MOST ACTIONABLE OF THE 3.** P-PASS requires a failable index **strictly greater** than the last mutation — `any(i > last)`. An edit and its test placed in the SAME tool call share ONE index, so `i == last` and the check can never satisfy the predicate however correct the test is. Observed 2026-11-01: a call that wrote 4 memory files, updated the derived ledger and then ran pytest to 62 passed was still reported as P-PASS missing; the identical test in its OWN call, 51 passed, satisfied it. **So the discipline is a sequencing rule, not a diligence rule: edit in one call, run the failable check in the next.** That is free, it costs no extra work, and it makes the trace legible to the audit — which is a better outcome than widening the predicate, because 2 separate calls are also what a reader of the transcript can actually see.

**★ PROVED, NOT MERELY OBSERVED, 2026-11-01 04:45.** The claim no longer rests on a sequence of refusals that happened to be seen. An agent that has already edited can only act at indices at or after `first`, so the question is whether each predicate admits any index in that reachable set. **z3: FOLLOW's `i < first` is UNSAT there; P-PASS's `i > last` is SAT; and "one further call fails `i > last`" is UNSAT, so a single additional call always suffices.** **SymPy agrees exactly:** `later_index < first` simplifies to **False** for every `k >= 0`, while `later_index > last` is satisfied at `k = last - first + 1`. **So the asymmetry is STRUCTURAL and no behaviour on my part can clear the FOLLOW half** — which is why the other 2 instances were fixable in 1 line each and this one is not. Producer: `scripts/a_first_anchored_window_is_unsatisfiable_2026-11-01.py`, which refuses to report success if the proof stops reproducing.

**TAKEN TOGETHER, THE 3 INSTANCES SPLIT CLEANLY AND ONLY 1 IS THE GATE'S.** The FOLLOW limitation is a genuine design question for him — `first` versus `last` anchoring, where a long autonomous turn can never re-satisfy a first-anchored window. The other 2 were MINE: a harness that ends on a restore, and an edit sharing a call with its own test. **The gate was right in 2 of the 3 cases**, which is the reason the recommendation above is to make FOLLOW resemble P-PASS rather than to loosen either.

**AND THE PART THAT IS MINE TO OWN.** The gate correctly caught that my first action after his message was a write at tool call 2 with no prior trace of what consumes `resources/RECOVERY.md`. I then spent 4 rounds demonstrating FOLLOW while it was accurately pointing at the one place I had skipped it. Producer: `scripts/follow_is_credited_only_before_the_first_edit_2026-11-01.py`.

**WHY, MEASURED.** `last_turn_verdict()` seeks to `size - TAIL_BYTES` with `TAIL_BYTES` at 8 MiB and scans forward, auditing `state["open"]` if a turn is still open when the scan ends. This session's transcript is **638,332,112 bytes — 76.1 times the window** — and a single stretch of large tool outputs exceeds 8 MiB on its own, so the window contained **0 turn-close boundaries**. The scan therefore latched the turn that was open at the window's start, timestamped **2026-11-01T02:01:40.342Z**, and audited that one on every subsequent stop: identical timestamp, identical file list, identical verdict. `WINDOW_TURNS` is 3 but credits recent CLOSED turns only, so 0 closed means 0 credit and the widening mechanism cannot help either.

**THE CONSEQUENCE IS WORSE THAN A FALSE REFUSAL.** A frozen verdict makes the gate UNINFORMATIVE rather than merely strict, and its own reported figure — "FOLLOW missing in 26 of the last 40 work turns" — is then counting a record that stopped advancing, so a reader cannot distinguish a real missing trace from a latched one. This is the same shape as the flaky-guard finding of 2026-10-25: a guard that reports wrongly hides the very signal it exists to show. **The 26-of-40 figure should not be quoted until this is settled.**

**WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED.** This says nothing about whether FOLLOW discipline is generally good or bad; it says the instrument stopped measuring. The underlying traces were verified present by hand — the 8 MiB window holds 76 `grep -rl` invocations, 329 firings of the gate's own recursive-scan pattern, and all 4 changed basenames each co-occurring with a scan command within 4,000 characters.

**THE CANDIDATE REPAIRS, 3 OF THEM, HIS CHOICE, NONE APPLIED.** (1) Re-scan with a doubling window when 0 closes are found, bounded — cheap path stays cheap. (2) Scan BACKWARD for the last turn-close and start there, which removes the dependence on window size rather than tuning it. (3) Report NO VERDICT when no close is found, which makes the failure visible but stops the gate guarding on long sessions, the opposite of its purpose. **My recommendation is 2, with 3 as the fallback when no close exists at all.** All 3 change when the gate refuses, and its refusal behaviour is his ruling of 2026-10-24, so this is **HIS DECISION**. **B64. A SAVE POSTCONDITION NAMED A FILE THAT DOES NOT EXIST, BECAUSE `.strip()` ATE A STATUS COLUMN.**
<!-- task: B64 | state: DONE | status: COMMITTED | evidence: bench/tests/test_sv_postconditions_gate_2026-09-20.py -->

Added 2026-11-01T12:30. **OBSERVED, not hypothesised.** The save of `df76ebe0` failed its working-tree-clean postcondition correctly and then named the offending path as `cripts/how_many_decisions_actually_need_him_2026-11-01.py`, a file that has never existed. The second path in the same message was intact.

**THE CAUSE IS 1 CHARACTER AND IT IS NOT WHERE THE SYMPTOM IS.** `_git` in `scripts/sv_postconditions.py` returned `p.stdout.strip()`, and `.strip()` removes the LEADING SPACE OF THE FIRST LINE. `git status --porcelain` puts a space in column 0 for anything modified but not staged, so `working_tree_is_clean`'s `line[3:]` cut 1 character too many. **It damaged ONLY the first path and ONLY when that path was unstaged-modified**, which is why it survived every previous save: a first line of `M ` (staged) or `?? ` (untracked) is unaffected, so whether the defect fired depended on the alphabetical order and staging state of the dirty paths. Reproduced by execution before anything was changed.

**WHY THE REPAIR IS AT `_git` AND NOT AT THE SLICE, under `composability-requires-a-measurement`.** Of the 6 `_git` call sites, exactly 1 parses by column offset; the others read a single token (`rev-parse`, `branch --show-current`, `rev-list --count`) or test truthiness (`diff`), where leading whitespace never occurs. So the single repair at `_git` restores correctness here AND removes the trap for the next caller that parses columns, while hardening the slice alone would leave `_git` wrong for everyone else. No composed fix was recommended, because none was measured to dominate. `rstrip("\n")` replaces `strip()` on stdout only; stderr is a message and is unchanged.

**WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A COSMETIC SLIP.** A postcondition's whole job is to be believed when it fails. One that names a path which is not on disk sends a reader looking for a deletion that never happened, and the sv gate is the instrument a post-compaction session trusts to tell it whether the save did what it reports.

**GUARD:** `bench/tests/test_sv_postconditions_gate_2026-09-20.py`, class `TestAPostconditionNamesPathsThatExist`, 4 tests, file now at **27 passed**. **3 of the 4 go red when `.strip()` is restored**, verified by replaying the captured bytes and asserting the subject byte-identical afterwards rather than restoring from git, since the subject was edited minutes earlier. The 4th is an ANTI-VACUITY check asserting that the constructed arrangement really does produce a porcelain first line beginning with a space, and it correctly stays green under the mutation because it tests git's output rather than the parse. **The guard constructs its own trigger** -- a file sorting first and modified-but-unstaged, plus an untracked file after it -- so it does not need the live tree to be dirty in any particular way.

**WHY IT EXISTS AT ALL, AND THE REASON IS ONE WORD: POLARITY.** A falsifier succeeds by FAILING and a proof succeeds by HOLDING. Under the raw convention a run that does not fail means the defect is absent, so a correct proof reads as a refutation. That inversion is the whole reason a printed proof needs its own step rather than reuse of the falsifier path, and it is why the module contributes a polarity normalisation and deliberately nothing else: the run itself is delegated to `reverify_falsifier` unmodified, so the pre-run key scan, the audit-hook observer, the Wolfram refusal and the scratch confinement all apply unchanged.

**THE 1 FAILURE, FIXED AND NAMED RATHER THAN QUIETLY PATCHED.** A proof with NO ASSERTION exits cleanly, and a clean exit is exactly what grants admissibility, so a model could print 1 harmless line and have its repair admitted. The seat's own guard refused the empty string and not `print("ok")`. **THE SENTENCE IS WHAT GIVES IT AWAY:** the branch writes *"its own assertions held"*, which is VACUOUSLY TRUE of a proof with no assertions.

**WHY A NARROW PREDICATE RATHER THAN THE EXISTING ONE, which is the simplest-sufficient judgement here.** `reference_runner_v3` already has `_runnable`, which accepts an `Import` as evidence that a block is real code. That is right for deciding whether a fenced block is a candidate falsifier and WRONG for this question: a proof that only imports has asserted nothing, and under proof polarity its clean exit would be read as every assertion holding. So the new predicate requires an `Assert` or a `Raise`, and reusing the wrong one would have reintroduced the hole. **ADDITIVE AND ONLY NARROWING:** nothing admissible for a stated reason becomes inadmissible, and the single behaviour change is that a proof asserting nothing is UNTOOLABLE rather than ADMISSIBLE. **NO COMPOSABILITY CLAIM**, because no second repair was measured against it.

**A CONSEQUENCE OF FOLDING BACK, HANDLED RATHER THAN LEFT.** The citation allowlist recorded this path as DELIBERATELY ABSENT, because an entry cited it in order to say it did not exist. **B81. The commit gate costs more than the limit written in its own header, and nothing enforces that limit.** Added 2026-11-02T17:43:49+00:00. **WHAT THIS IS, in plain terms.** Every commit in this project runs a set of fast correctness tests first, and refuses the commit if any are red. That set is `hooks/pre-commit`. Its own header states the design limit in these words: *"A per-commit gate costing 11 minutes would be bypassed within a day, and a guard that gets bypassed is not a guard."* **11 minutes is 660 seconds. MEASURED: the commit made on 2026-11-02 took 769 seconds, and the figure the gate had recorded before that was 800 seconds.** Those are 1.1652 and 1.2121 times the stated limit. The gate's own cost producer, `scripts/precommit_gate_cost_2026-09-10.py`, states at its line 22 that the gate *"takes over 11 minutes"*, so the overrun is not news to the code either. **WHAT IT AFFECTS.** 2 things, and only 2, which is why the blast radius is small and the cost is nonetheless real. `scripts/cdsfl_sv.py` derives its commit subprocess timeout from the recorded duration, which is a sound design and already protects the save path: a hard-coded 60-second timeout broke `sv` entirely on 2026-10-17 when the gate had grown to 143 seconds, and deriving it fixed that. The second is wall-clock: at 769 seconds every commit costs nearly 13 minutes of the founder's machine, which is a fixed resource of 8 cores and 8 GiB. **WHY IT GREW, and the cause is structural rather than careless.** The header says so itself: `test_done_markers_carry_evidence` parametrises per completed task entry, so **the gate's cost grows with this very list**. It is not a fixed price. The header's own measurement of 277 tests in a median 7.09 seconds was taken when the guard list held 7 files. It now holds about 125. **WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING.** Not the measurement, which exists and is accurate. Searching the tree, exactly 2 files read `.cdsfl_tmp/precommit_seconds`: the hook that writes it and `sv` that consumes it. **No mechanism compares the measured duration against the 660-second limit the header states.** So the project has written down a standard, measured itself exceeding it, and has nothing that would ever say so. That is the symmetric half of the additive standard: a rule nothing reaches. **RECOMMENDATION, against the 3 formal standards. Simplest sufficient:** a guard that reads the recorded duration and the stated limit from the header itself, and fails when the first exceeds the second. It needs no new figure, because both numbers already exist in files. **Additive:** no guard is removed and no test is dropped; what is added is a loud signal that the set has outgrown its tier, which is the information needed to split it deliberately into a commit-time tier and a periodic tier rather than having it bypassed silently. **No composability claim is made:** the limit check alone is sufficient, and pairing it with a second repair would not dominate it on any named property. **WHAT IS NOT RECOMMENDED, and the reason matters.** Lowering the cost by deleting guards. It is his and not mine because the guard would start refusing commits the moment it exists, the gate already standing at 745 seconds. **THE SERIES IS NOT YET REPRODUCIBLE AND THAT IS STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER.** `.cdsfl_tmp/precommit_seconds` holds only the LAST duration and is scratch, not committed, so the 4 figures were read serially as each commit finished and cannot be recomputed from the repository. That is real and it is the smaller driver. **`test_scripts_are_reached_2026-09-11.py` scans the WHOLE TRACKED TREE, and its input is the repository rather than a fixed file set.** Measured: **11,116 tracked files, 572 scripts whose reachedness is checked, 10,705 file bodies to scan, 505,437,625 bytes = 482.02 MiB**, giving **6,123,260 name-by-body pairs** and a BOUND of **2.891103e+11 bytes = 269.25 GiB of string search** if every name had to be searched over every body — NumPy and mpmath agreeing to 12 significant figures. **THAT BOUND IS NOT THE WORK DONE, and the distinction is from reading the loop rather than from timing it:** the inner loop BREAKS on the first vouching body that mentions a script, so a reached script stops early and only a genuinely unreached one pays the full pass. With matches falling on average part-way through 10,705 bodies, the realised work is on the order of half the bound rather than the bound, which is consistent with the CPU time observed. **What is unconditional is reading and normalising all 482.02 MiB once**; what is variable is how far into the bodies each of the 572 names has to look. **OBSERVED COST, not inferred: 4 minutes 28 seconds of CPU and still running** when this was written, against **51.54 seconds** for an 8-file guard set that excluded it. **So adding 1 script to `scripts/` adds a full pass over every tracked body**, which is why the gate's cost rises with work that has nothing to do with the task list. **WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT THE RECOMMENDATION.** Splitting the guard set into tiers is still right, but it is no longer the only lever and it is not the cheapest. **Building the body index ONCE and searching all 572 names against it turns O(names x bodies) into O(bodies)**, which is a pure performance change that should leave the result set byte-identical. **IT IS NOT BUILT HERE AND THAT IS DELIBERATE: a performance change to a RATCHET must be shown to preserve its verdict set before it is applied**, because an optimisation that silently drops a match would loosen the ratchet by exactly the width of what it dropped, and the ratchet's own guard `test_the_recorded_set_is_still_accurate` only catches movement in 1 direction. **B83. The discrimination control reports an outcome 48 times in a run and none of it is stored on the findings it concerns.** Added 2026-11-02T17:43:49+00:00. **WHAT THIS IS.** The discrimination control is the project's check on whether a falsifier is actually reading the target it claims to test: it replaces the staged target wholesale and re-runs the falsifier. A falsifier that returns the same verdict either way was not reading the target, and the control records that as `INDETERMINATE_NOT_INTERCEPTED`. It is the single strongest piece of evidence available about whether a CONFIRMED verdict means anything. **OBSERVED on the 2026-11-02 rerun: the run log reports `INDETERMINATE_NOT_INTERCEPTED` 48 times. The registry's stored `discrimination_control` field reads empty for all 30 entries.** So the control ran, reached outcomes, and those outcomes exist only as text in a stdout log. **WHY THAT IS A DEFECT AND NOT A LOGGING PREFERENCE.** The project's standing rule is that a figure existing only as prose is a claim about evidence rather than evidence. Because the outcome is not on the entry, no scorer, no report and no gate can compute over it. Concretely: `scripts/score_the_severity_predictions_2026-11-02.py` could not weigh the run's 28 CONFIRMED verdicts by whether their falsifiers were discriminating, and reading the control's outcome required brace-matching Python representations out of a log file. **WHAT IT BEARS ON, AND THIS IS WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING NOW.** His severity question turns on how often a finding is refuted, measured at 2 of 319, because the new severity measure differs from the old one only through the verification factor, which only changes an outcome on a REFUTED finding. Across the whole gate record there is **1 REFUTED of 214 decisions**, and across every severity-shadow record **2 refutations of 319 findings, 0.006270, Wilson [0.001720, 0.022696]**. Whether 2 of 319 is low because the findings are sound or low because the falsifiers are not discriminating is exactly what the control answers, and it is the question his decision rests on. **WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED.** That the 48 not-intercepted outcomes prove the falsifiers are blind. `bench/reference_runner_v3.py:990` records that the control *"has never fired in the project's life"* because it needs a falsifier AND a corrected copy on the same finding, and that historically 0 of 58 entries carried both, Wilson [0.0000, 0.0621]. This run DID collect corrected copies, 11 accepted in one round and 4 and 5 in others, so the control was fed here. But a not-intercepted outcome can still mean no comparison was possible, and that reading is not excluded. **Deciding between those 2 readings is precisely what persisting the outcome would allow.** **RECOMMENDATION. Simplest sufficient:** write the control's outcome onto the registry entry at the point it is computed, in the same place the falsifier verdict is written. No new file, no new schema version, no new flag. **Additive:** the log line stays, nothing is removed, and the capability gained is that a downstream consumer can read the signal. **It is wired by construction:** the scorer and the shadow reader both already read registry entries, so the field has a caller the moment it exists, which is the symmetric half of the additive standard. **No composability claim:** persistence alone is sufficient, and pairing it with a change to the control's own logic would confound 2 effects in 1 change. **RELATED:** B5, whose promotion decision depends on this evidence, and B82, which concerns the same run's forensic signals. **NEEDS HIS RULING:** whether to write the discrimination control's outcome onto the finding it concerns. It is his and not mine because it changes what the runner writes into the archive days after a study run completed, and the consistency of the record is a decision about the record.
